description: NASA collects billions of bytes of Earth data every day, but complex graphs and charts are often inaccessible or boring to the general public. Our team is bridging the gap between hard science and human emotion by translating NASA’s Earth observation data into interactive, immersive soundscapes. We aren't just building a dashboard; we are building a musical instrument powered by the planet.
summary: Earth Jukebox is a web app that lets people hear NASA Earth science instead of only seeing it. Click a city on an interactive globe and NASA’s GEOS-CF air-quality model plays as music: fine particles (PM2.5), ozone, carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide become four instruments, and dirtier air sounds faster, higher and more tense. You can also pick a NASA Earth Information Center image, such as the Air Quality Model Runs globe, the 2024 temperature anomaly map or the Arctic sea ice minimum, and a scanning line turns its colours, brightness and shapes into a soundscape in real time. Every record comes with a text description, spoken announcements and full keyboard control, so blind and low-vision users can explore it. It answers the challenge by pairing EIC visuals with dynamic sonification, and it matters because air pollution and climate data should be accessible to everyone.
details:
Earth Jukebox has two kinds of records. For data records, a Python script pulls hourly surface-level GEOS-CF output (PM2.5, ozone, CO and NO2) from NASA’s OPeNDAP service, averages it over a box around each of 13 cities, and saves it as a small file, so the demo never depends on a live server. In the browser, each pollutant drives one instrument that is synthesized live. PM2.5 is a kick-drum beat that subdivides at each US EPA health band and hits harder when the air is dirtier, with a quiet click marking the WHO guideline. Ozone is a bell in the left ear, CO is a pad, and NO2 is light ticks in the right ear. Values are scaled against health-based ranges rather than each city’s own minimum and maximum, so a clean city and a polluted city sound clearly different.

For image records, we load NASA EIC and Scientific Visualization Studio frames and a line sweeps left to right. Each slice’s hue picks a bass note, its brightness opens the filter of a pad, and the height of its most striking feature sets the melody pitch, panned with the scan. Sharp edges add light ticks. The image’s overall colour sets the key, with warm images leaning minor and cool images major. Notes come from musical scales so the result is pleasant rather than noisy. People can also load their own image.

Accessibility: Each record has a written description, a “Describe this moment” button, optional live announcements while playing, full keyboard shortcuts, labelled controls for screen readers, a high-contrast mode, and the Atkinson Hyperlegible typeface, which was designed for low-vision readers. A guided tour plays a short sequence on its own.

Benefits and impact: It makes Earth Information Center content reachable for blind and low-vision users, and it lets anyone feel the difference between clean and polluted air in seconds. We started with Kathmandu Valley, where winter air pollution is a serious local issue. More places can be added by giving a latitude and longitude box, so it can grow to a global jukebox.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with the Web Audio API (all sound is synthesized live, with no audio files) and Canvas for the globe and charts. Python (xarray, netCDF4, pandas, numpy) extracts the data. We used NASA GEOS-CF data, SVS visualizations 5533 (Air Quality Model Runs), 5450 (global temperature anomaly) and 5382 (Arctic sea ice minimum), and Natural Earth land outlines (public domain). It runs in an ordinary browser with headphones or speakers, and needs no special hardware.

Creativity: The jukebox idea becomes a globe you spin and pictures you choose like sleeves in a rack. We offer two honest ways to translate Earth data: measured values and the picture itself. Rule-based musical mappings let a team without musicians produce music that sounds good.

Factors we considered: Accessibility came first. We were open about the difference between the two modes: image mode is an artistic reading of a picture’s colours, not a measurement, while data mode plays real model values, and the app says so. We balanced musicality against data fidelity, scaled pollutants by health thresholds, and pre-extracted the data for reliability. The data are model values at roughly 0.25 degree resolution averaged over a city-sized box, not ground-sensor readings, and each record covers the time window we fetched.

AI use: We used AI assistance (Claude by Anthropic) to help write and refine code, the interface design and these descriptions. The team chose the concept, data and sound mappings, and ran and tested the result.
